name: LLM-as-a-Judge
question: Is this output actually good?
summary: A strong model grades outputs against a written rubric. It scales human-like judgment to thousands of cases for qualities code can’t check: helpfulness, tone, soundness of reasoning and policy compliance.
useCases: Open-ended outputs with no single right answer
Fast prompt iteration where human review would be the bottleneck
Continuous monitoring of sampled production traffic

items.detail: score one output on pass/fail or a 1–5 scale
pick the better of outputs A and B
% agreement or Cohen’s κ on a labelled sample

steps: Write a rubric with concrete criteria and an example for each score
Ask the judge to reason first, then give the score
Prefer binary or 3-point scales, which are more consistent than 1–10
Label 50–100 cases by hand and check agreement before trusting the judge
pitfalls: Position bias: in pairwise mode, run both orders
Verbosity bias: longer answers score higher unless the rubric says otherwise
Self-preference: judge with a different model family where possible
remember: Rubric first, reasoning before score, calibrate against humans.
caption: The judge sees the output and the rubric, writes its reasoning, then scores.

code.text: Pass only if the summary states the correct payout amount,
names the damage, and invents nothing.
Pass example: "Kitchen water damage approved; INR 42,000."
"Explain your reasoning, then end with SCORE: 0 or 1.")

steps.title: Write the rubric
steps.text: Concrete criteria plus an example for each score. Binary pass/fail is more consistent than a 1–10 scale.

steps.title: Send output and rubric to the judge
steps.text: Use a strong model, ideally from a different family than the one being judged, at temperature 0.

steps.title: Reason first, then score
steps.text: Ask for reasoning before the verdict and parse only the final score. Keep the reasoning for audits.

steps.title: Guard against position bias
steps.text: For pairwise comparisons, judge both orders. Count a win only if both agree; otherwise call it a tie.

steps.title: Calibrate against people
steps.text: Hand-label a sample and measure agreement and Cohen's κ. Here the judge agrees with people on 8 of 10.

pros: Scales human-like judgment to thousands of outputs
Handles open-ended qualities code can’t check
Far cheaper and faster than human review
Easy to start: a rubric and a prompt
cons: Must be calibrated against human labels
Verdicts drift when the judge model changes
Adds a model call per evaluated item
avoidWhen: An exact check exists in code (use that instead)
High-stakes decisions with no human review

tools.name: DeepEval (G-Eval)
tools.what: Plain-language criteria turned into judge metrics

tools.name: autoevals
tools.what: Ready-made judge scorers such as factuality

playgroundGuide.scenario: A judge model is grading two summaries of the same insurance claim. A is short and correct. B is long and polite, but states the wrong payout. A human reviewer prefers A. Configure the judge so it agrees with the human, for the right reasons.
controls: Show B first: which answer the judge reads first.
Position bias: the judge favours whichever answer it sees first (+0.3).
Rubric rule: the rubric says length earns nothing, which removes the +0.5 verbosity bonus.
Run both orders: judge A-then-B and B-then-A, and accept a winner only if both agree.

outputs.name: Judge scores
outputs.meaning: Simulated score for each answer: quality plus any bias bonuses.

outputs.name: Verdict
outputs.meaning: Which answer the judge picks, and whether that matches the human.

presets.name: Naive judge
presets.expect: B shown first, biased, no rubric rule. Expect the judge to pick B, the wrong answer.

presets.name: Add a rubric rule
presets.expect: Removing the verbosity bonus lets A win, but only narrowly while B is shown first.

presets.name: Production setup
presets.expect: Rubric rule plus both orders. A wins consistently, whatever the order.

presets.name: Inconsistent judge
presets.expect: No rubric rule but both orders checked. The verdict flips with the order, so it’s reported as a tie for a person to review.

missions.text: Make the judge pick A without switching off position bias.
missions.hint: Turn on the rubric rule, or show A first.

missions.text: Make the judge report a tie.
missions.hint: Keep the verbosity bonus and run both orders.

missions.text: Make A win by a clear margin of 0.5 or more.
missions.hint: Rubric rule on, and A shown first so position bias helps it.

tools.best: Write a criterion in plain English and get a scored metric with a pass threshold and the judge’s reasoning.
tools.ex: A “Correctness” metric that fails any claim summary with a wrong payout amount.
cons: Scores shift when you change judge models

tools.best: Rubric assertions inside YAML test suites, next to exact-match checks.
tools.ex: An assertion: “mentions the payout amount and invents nothing”, run on 100 summaries in CI.
pros: Mix rubric and exact checks in one suite
cons: Less control over the judge prompt
Long rubrics get awkward in YAML

tools.best: Prebuilt judge scorers such as Factuality and ClosedQA that you call from code.
tools.ex: Factuality(output, expected) returns a score and rationale for each claim summary.
pros: Tested judge prompts ready to use
Works on its own or with Braintrust
cons: Generic prompts may not fit your domain

tools.best: Templates that show how model-graded evals are structured.
tools.ex: Study a model-graded template before writing your own rubric prompt.

tools.best: Measuring judge–human agreement with cohen_kappa_score and confusion matrices.
tools.ex: Each week, compare 100 human labels with judge labels and report κ on a dashboard.
cons: Measures agreement; it doesn’t judge anything

goals: Write a rubric with anchored examples for each score
Name three judge biases and how to counter each
Measure judge–human agreement and explain why κ matters

practice.scenario: An insurer produces about 2,000 claim-summary emails a week. A judge model scores each one for accuracy, completeness and tone against a written rubric. Each week, 100 are also scored by people, to confirm the judge still agrees with them before its scores are trusted.

industries.use: Grade claim summaries and customer letters for accuracy and tone
Score tutoring answers for correctness and clarity
Monitor sampled live replies for policy compliance

practice.analogy: A senior teacher marking essays against a published marking scheme, while the head of department re-marks a sample to keep the scores honest.

library.name: DeepEval
library.what: Pytest-style LLM testing. G-Eval turns a plain-language criterion into a judge metric with a pass threshold.

samples.code:
from deepeval import evaluate
from deepeval.metrics import GEval
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase, LLMTestCaseParams

correctness = GEval(
    name="Correctness",
    criteria="Is the actual output factually consistent with the expected output? "
             "Penalize missing amounts or invented details.",
    evaluation_params=[LLMTestCaseParams.ACTUAL_OUTPUT,
                       LLMTestCaseParams.EXPECTED_OUTPUT],
    threshold=0.7,
)

case = LLMTestCase(
    input="Summarize claim CLM-004471 for the customer",
    actual_output="Water damage to your kitchen is covered. Payout: INR 42,000.",
    expected_output="Kitchen water damage approved. Payout INR 42,000.",
)
evaluate(test_cases=[case], metrics=[correctness])

numericDrill.question: Your judge and a human labelled 10 answers pass/fail and agreed on 8. What is the percent agreement, and why can it overstate the judge's quality?
numericDrill.answer: Agreement = 8 ÷ 10 = 80%. Percent agreement ignores agreement by chance: if most labels are “pass”, a judge that always says pass agrees often. Cohen's κ corrects for chance.

interview.question: Which biases affect LLM judges, and how do you reduce them?
interview.answer: Position bias (run both orders), verbosity bias (state in the rubric that length earns nothing), and self-preference (judge with a different model family). Always calibrate against a human-labelled sample.

interview.question: Why prefer binary or 3-point scales over 1–10?
interview.answer: Models are inconsistent at fine-grained scores; the same answer drifts between 6 and 8. Coarse scales with anchored examples are more repeatable and easier to calibrate against people.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for the score before the reasoning
mistakes.fix: Ask for reasoning first, then the score

mistakes.mistake: Trusting the judge without human spot checks
mistakes.fix: Hand-label 50–100 cases and re-check agreement regularly

quiz.question: For weekly claim emails, which check should go to an LLM judge rather than code?
options: The payout equals the ledger value
The tone is empathetic and the next steps are clear
The email contains the claim ID
quiz.explanation: Use code for exact facts and a judge for open-ended qualities like tone and clarity.

quiz.question: Which are well-documented LLM-judge biases? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Position, verbosity and self-preference biases are well documented.

quiz.question: Comparing two product-description generators, the judge prefers whichever answer it reads first. What is the fix?
options: Judge both orders and count a win only if they agree
quiz.explanation: If the winner changes with the order, it is not a real preference.

quiz.question: Which scoring scale gives the most consistent judge scores for complaint replies?
options: Pass/fail or 3 points, with an example for each score
quiz.explanation: Coarse scales anchored with examples are more repeatable.

quiz.question: The judge and teachers agree 80% of the time on a set where 80% of answers are good. What is the concern?
options: A judge that always says “good” would also get 80%, so check Cohen’s κ
Add more examples to the rubric
quiz.explanation: Percent agreement ignores chance. κ corrects for it.

quiz.question: Which are good rubric practices for grading claim summaries? Select all that apply.
options: Stating that length earns no credit
quiz.explanation: Vague instructions produce vague, biased scores.

quiz.question: You are grading outputs from Model X. Which judge should you use?
options: A strong model from a different family
quiz.explanation: A different model family reduces self-preference bias.

quiz.question: Why ask the judge for its reasoning before the score?
options: It makes scores more considered and gives a trail to audit
quiz.explanation: Reasoning first improves scores and leaves something a person can review.

quiz.question: The judge model is upgraded and scores rise 6 points overnight. What should you do?
options: Re-calibrate the new judge on the human-labelled set before comparing
quiz.explanation: A new judge is a new ruler. Check it against people first.

quiz.question: The judge gives long support replies higher scores even when the extra text adds nothing. What is happening, and what helps?
options: Verbosity bias; say in the rubric that length earns nothing and compare against a reference
quiz.explanation: Judges tend to reward length. Tell the judge explicitly that length earns no credit.

quiz.question: The judge rates confident but medically wrong answers highly. What is the best fix?
options: Give the judge a vetted reference answer and route high-risk topics to clinician review
quiz.explanation: Judges can be fooled by fluent answers. Reference-guided grading plus expert review guards high-stakes content.

quiz.question: Which calibration set is best before trusting a judge on contract Q&A?
options: About 200 real outputs labelled by two domain experts, including failures
20 outputs labelled by the prompt engineer
quiz.explanation: Calibrate on real, expert-labelled data that includes the failures you care about.

quiz.question: Agreement between the judge and human reviewers is κ = 0.25. Should you trust the judge?
options: No: agreement is weak; tighten the rubric and add examples, then measure again
Yes, if the judge is a large model
quiz.explanation: κ around 0.2–0.4 is only fair agreement. Improve the rubric before relying on the judge.

quiz.question: What temperature should a judge run at?
options: 0 or very low, for repeatable scores
As high as possible, to reduce bias
quiz.explanation: You want the same input to get the same score.

quiz.question: The judge’s scores are stable week to week, but disagreement with the human spot-check has risen from 10% to 25%. What should you do?
options: Trust the judge: it is stable
Re-calibrate: the product or the answer mix has drifted from what the rubric was tuned on
quiz.explanation: The weekly human sample exists to catch exactly this drift.

quiz.question: You must choose between two prompt versions for tutoring answers. Which judging set-up fits best?
options: Pairwise comparison, judged in both orders
One absolute score from a single run
Asking the tutor model which it prefers
quiz.explanation: Pairwise judging is sensitive to small differences. Swapping the order controls position bias.

quiz.question: Which rubric criteria are concrete enough for a judge? Select all that apply.
options: States the payout amount exactly as in the claim record
States the next step and its date
quiz.explanation: Criteria must be checkable. “Good” and “nice” mean different things to different graders.

quiz.question: Each week, 2,000 emails are judged at $0.01 each, and 100 are also reviewed by people at $0.50 each. What is the weekly cost?
The judge must return JSON {score, reason}, but 3% of its replies cannot be parsed. What is the right handling?
options: Use structured output or validate and retry, and track parse failures separately
quiz.explanation: Parse failures are an eval-infrastructure bug. They should not quietly shift the scores.

quiz.question: Your judge and your generator are the same model, and judge scores run 8 points above human ratings. What is the likely cause?
options: Self-preference; use a judge from a different family and re-calibrate
quiz.explanation: Models tend to rate their own style highly.
